issues.legal_issue: A presumptive reversioner who knowingly assents to, adopts, or ratifies a widow’s otherwise voidable alienation cannot later challenge it upon succession opening.
material_facts: The widows held only a widow’s estate, and the challenged alienations were not made for necessity of the estate, so the alienations were prima facie not binding on reversioners.

One presumptive reversioner, with knowledge of the existing alienations, accepted an agreement affirming them and obtained substantial property; he later dealt with property received under that agreement.

Other presumptive reversioners were minors when their guardian entered into an arrangement under which they received property. After attaining majority, they retained and dealt with that property rather than renouncing the arrangement.
The agreements and subsequent dealings showed that the presumptive reversioners accepted the arrangements and the benefits they provided.
issues.conclusion: The plaintiffs were precluded from challenging the alienations. An alienation by a Hindu widow is voidable, not void, and a reversioner who assents to or ratifies it, or elects to retain benefits under the relevant transaction, cannot later repudiate it.
issues.legal_principle: Under Hindu law, an alienation by a widow in excess of her powers is voidable at the instance of the reversioners, who may be precluded from avoiding it by express assent, conduct treating it as valid, election, or ratification. A presumptive reversioner has no vested right before succession opens but may elect to stand by or ratify a transaction. A minor cannot be compelled to accept a benefit that would deprive the minor of later legal rights; after attaining majority, however, the minor may ratify the guardian’s transaction, and continued enjoyment of a benefit originally conferred on the minor may itself suffice. The Court relied on Ramgouda Annagouda v. Bhausaheb, T. V. R. Subbu Chetty’s Family Charities v. M. Raghava Mudaliar, Fateh Singh v. Thakur Rukmini Ramanji Maharaj, Jagarlapudi Seetharamayya v. Sarva Chandrayya, Makineni Virayya v. Madamanchi Bapayya, and Krishna Beharilal v. Gulab Chand; it also discussed the categories of estoppel under section 115 of the Evidence Act.

rule.if: reversioner_challenges_widow_alienation and (knowingly_assented_to_alienation or (minor_when_benefit_received and attained_majority and retained_and_dealt_with_benefit))

predicates.reversioner_challenges_widow_alienation: A person claiming as a reversioner seeks to challenge an alienation made by a widow holding a limited estate.
predicates.knowingly_assented_to_alienation: The presumptive reversioner, knowing of the alienation, accepted or affirmed its validity in a transaction.
predicates.minor_when_benefit_received: The presumptive reversioner was a minor when a guardian entered into a transaction conferring a benefit on that minor.
predicates.attained_majority: The presumptive reversioner later attained legal majority.
predicates.retained_and_dealt_with_benefit: After attaining majority, the presumptive reversioner retained the benefit and dealt with it as the recipient of the transaction.

issues.definition: When a reversioner challenging a widow’s alienation knowingly assented to it, or as a minor later retained and dealt with a benefit from the transaction, the reversioner is precluded from challenging the alienation.

issues.legal_issue: Agreements between near relations that settle actual or possible disputes in good faith to secure family peace may constitute binding family arrangements even without conflicting vested legal claims.
material_facts: The parties were near relations and had disputes concerning property and claims that would arise when succession opened.
An agreement gave one branch of the family immediate possession of property, while recognizing the widows’ rights to other property and to manage charitable properties.
A later agreement, made after litigation over a purported will, provided property to a presumptive reversioner and recognized the rights of the widows and other recipients of earlier alienations.
The beneficiaries of the agreements subsequently retained and dealt with property received under them.
issues.conclusion: The agreements, read together, constituted a family arrangement, and the plaintiffs could not repudiate the arrangements after accepting their benefits.
issues.legal_principle: Courts favor bona fide family arrangements that bring about harmony, settle actual or possible disputes, and avoid future litigation. A conflict of present or future legal claims is generally relevant but is not indispensable; bona fide disputes between near relations, even disputes not involving legal claims, may suffice. A family arrangement may be inferred from a long course of dealings, and courts are more ready to uphold an agreement made bona fide on fair terms than to avoid it. The Court relied on Sahu Madho Das v. Pandit Mukand Ram, Maturi Pullaiah v. Maturi Narasimhan, Krishna Beharilal v. Gulab Chand, and Ram Charan Das v. Girjanandini Devi.

rule.if: family_arrangement_dispute and near_relations_disputed_property_claims and bona_fide_settlement_to_preserve_harmony and parties_accepted_transactional_benefits

predicates.family_arrangement_dispute: A proceeding disputes whether agreements settling family property claims are effective as a family arrangement.
predicates.near_relations_disputed_property_claims: Near relations had actual or possible disputes over property or claims arising in the future.
predicates.bona_fide_settlement_to_preserve_harmony: The parties entered into the arrangement in good faith to settle disputes, avoid litigation, or preserve family peace.
predicates.parties_accepted_transactional_benefits: The parties accepted benefits under the arrangement and acted on the transactions it established.

issues.definition: A bona fide settlement by near relations of actual or possible property disputes to preserve harmony is recognized as binding when the parties accept its benefits.

issues.legal_issue: A charitable dedication is complete only when the property is shown to have been devoted to the charity rather than retained as private property subject to a charitable charge.
material_facts: A settlement deed set properties apart for specified charities but also provided that any surplus after conducting the charities could be used for family expenses by the manager and heirs.
The plaintiffs claimed that the properties had been completely dedicated and that a trust for the charity had been created.
The plaintiffs did not provide acceptable evidence of the properties’ income, leaving no adequate basis to determine whether a substantial surplus remained after charitable expenses.
The evidence did not establish that the income was substantially intended for the charity or that only an insignificant portion could be used for the manager’s or worshipper’s maintenance.
issues.conclusion: The plaintiffs failed to establish a complete dedication. The dedication was treated as partial, the properties retained their private character subject to the charitable purpose, and the widows had a beneficial interest in them.
issues.legal_principle: A dedication to religious or charitable purposes may be complete or partial. Complete dedication creates a trust in favor of the charity; partial dedication creates a charge in favor of the charity while the property retains its private and secular character. Whether dedication is complete is a question of fact determined, where there is a document, by its fair and reasonable construction and the intention shown by it. If income is substantially intended for charity and only an insignificant portion is available for the manager’s or worshipper’s maintenance, complete dedication may be found; if only a minor portion is required for charity and a substantial surplus is available for private purposes, complete dedication is difficult to find. The party asserting complete dedication must establish it. The Court relied on Menakuru Dasaratharami Reddi v. Duddukuru Subba Rao and referred to Kalipada Chakraborti v. Palani Bala Devi.

predicates.complete_charitable_dedication_claim: A claimant asserts that property was completely dedicated to charitable purposes.
predicates.claimant_failed_to_establish_income_and_: The claimant did not establish the property income or show that the income was substantially intended for charity rather than leaving a substantial surplus for private use.

issues.definition: When a claimant asserting complete charitable dedication fails to establish the income and its substantial charitable use, the dedication is treated as partial and the property retains its private character.
